_description: Fixture 5 — Citation validation edge cases. Tests unverified citations, missing evidence linkage, and partially verified bibliography.
research_question: What are the key mechanisms by which exercise reduces cardiovascular disease risk?

report.executive_summary: Regular aerobic exercise reduces cardiovascular disease risk through multiple mechanisms including improved endothelial function, reduced systemic inflammation, and beneficial changes to lipid profiles. [SOURCE 1] [SOURCE 2]
key_findings: 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity exercise reduces cardiovascular mortality risk by 35%. [SOURCE 1]
Aerobic exercise increases HDL cholesterol by 3–6% and reduces LDL particle size in previously sedentary adults. [SOURCE 2]
Exercise reduces C-reactive protein (CRP) levels by 20–30% in individuals with elevated baseline inflammation. [SOURCE 3]
High-intensity interval training produces equivalent cardiovascular benefits to moderate continuous exercise in less total time. [SOURCE 4]
report.limitations: Optimal exercise dose varies by individual health status and age. Most studies are observational.

evidence.content: A meta-analysis of 36 cohort studies (n=1.2 million) found that individuals meeting the WHO physical activity guidelines of 150 min/week moderate exercise experienced 35% lower cardiovascular mortality vs. inactive individuals (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.59–0.72).
Systematic review of 40 RCTs found aerobic exercise training increased HDL-C by a mean of 4.6% (95% CI 2.6–6.5%) and reduced small, dense LDL particle count by 8% in previously sedentary adults.
Exercise intervention studies report 20–35% reductions in CRP levels among participants with baseline CRP > 3 mg/L following 12–24 weeks of regular moderate aerobic exercise.
A 12-week RCT comparing HIIT (3×20 min/week) to moderate continuous exercise (5×30 min/week) found equivalent VO2max improvements (HIIT: +9.3%, MICT: +9.1%, p=0.91) and similar lipid profile changes.
